Joost was the Process and Operations Manager and in early 2024

[2] Cataldo Miccio and Peter Win were non-executive directors of APP, appointed on 14
December 2018. Bruce Whall was also a non-executive director, appointed on 11 June 2024.
[3] Mr Miccio’s status as a non-executive director changed when he became acting CEO in
a limited capacity for part of 2024 through until APP went into liquidation.
[4] APP was a startup venture in the medicinal cannabis market. It was heavily reliant on
funding in the development phase of its business. It experienced funding difficulties through
the middle and end of 2024. APP went into voluntary administration on 20 November 2024 and
then into liquidation on 4 February 2025.
[5] Mr Joost’s employment was terminated on 23 October 2024. This was unrelated to the
funding difficulties that APP was experiencing.
[6] Mr Joost’s employment relationship problem arose out of his dismissal and the non-
payment of his salary immediately before and then after his dismissal, and the non-payment of
his accrued but untaken holiday entitlement. In respect of the alleged non-payments, Mr Joost’s
seeks payment from each of Mr Miccio, Mr Win and Mr Whall as persons involved in breaches
of employment standards pursuant to ss 142Y and 142W of Employment Relations Act 2000
(the Act).
[7] After APP went into liquidation the liquidators refused consent for Mr Joost to continue
with his claim against APP.
[8] Mr Joost continued with his claim against Mr Miccio, Mr Win and Mr Whall as persons
involved in breaches of employment standards. It is this claim that forms the employment
relationship problem that I investigated.
The Authority’s investigation
[9] I investigated this employment relationship problem by receiving written evidence and
documents, holding an investigation meeting on 20 March 2026 and assessing the written
submissions of the parties.
[10] In my investigation meeting, under oath or affirmation, witnesses confirmed their
statement and gave oral evidence in answer to questions from myself and the parties’
representatives.

[11] As permitted by s 174E of the Act I have not recorded all the evidence and submissions
received, in this determination. I have set out my findings of fact and law, then based on this I
have expressed conclusions on issues as necessary to dispose of the matter, and then I have
specified the orders made as a result.
Preliminary point
[12] The question of whether Mr Joost could continue with his employment relationship
problem with the three directors when he did not have permission from the liquidators to
proceed against APP was raised by counsel for Mr Miccio and Mr Win.
[13] This issue was resolved relatively easily with a discussion about Lawton v Steel Pencil
Holdings Ltd (in liquidation).1 In Lawton the Employment Court held that an employment
relationship problem based on s 142W of the Act could proceed against the individual defendant
in circumstances where the company was in liquidation and the liquidators did not consent to
the claim against the company proceeding. Counsel accepted this point and I proceeded with
my investigation.
Issues
[14] This employment relationship problem is based on Mr Joost seeking payment of his
unpaid salary and accrued holiday entitlements from Mr Miccio, Mr Win and/or Mr Whall. The
basis for this is that the failures by APP to pay these amounts are breaches of employment
standards and as such the payment can be sought from persons involved in the breaches of
employment standards pursuant to ss 142Y and 142W of the Act
[15] Section 142Y of the Act provides:
142YWhen person involved in breach liable for default in payment of
wages or other money due to employee
(1) A Labour Inspector or an employee may recover from a person who is not
the employee’s employer any wages or other money payable to the employee
if—
(a) there has been a default in the payment of wages or other money
payable to the employee; and
1 Lawton v Steel Pencil Holdings Ltd (in liquidation)[2021] NZEmpC 199.

(b) the default is due to a breach of employment standards; and
(c) the person is a person involved in the breach within the meaning
of section 142W.
(2) However, arrears in wages or other money may be recovered under
subsection (1) only,—
(a) in the case of recovery by an employee, with the prior leave of the
Authority or the court; and
(b) to the extent that the employee’s employer is unable to pay the
arrears in wages or other money.
[16] Section 142W of the Act provides:
142W Involvement in breaches
(1) In this Act, a person is involved in a breach if the breach is a breach of
employment standards and the person—
(a) has aided, abetted, counselled, or procured the breach; or
(b) has induced, whether by threats or promises or otherwise, the
breach; or
(c) has been in any way, directly or indirectly, knowingly concerned
in, or party to, the breach; or
(d) has conspired with others to effect the breach.
(2) However, if the breach is a breach by an entity such as a company,
partnership, limited partnership, or sole trader, a person who occupies a
position in the entity may be treated as a person involved in the breach only if
that person is an officer of the entity.
(3) For the purposes of subsection (2), the following persons are to be treated
as officers of an entity:
(a) a person occupying the position of a director of a company if the
entity is a company:
(b) a partner if the entity is a partnership:
(c) a general partner if the entity is a limited partnership:
(d) a person occupying a position comparable with that of a director of
a company if the entity is not a company, partnership, or limited
partnership:

(e) any other person occupying a position in the entity if the person is
in a position to exercise significant influence over the management or
administration of the entity.
(4) This section does not apply to proceedings for offences.
[17] A failure to pay money owed pursuant to an employment standard is a breach of that
standard. Section 142Y of the Act enables an employee to recover money (payable as an
employment standard) from a person who is not the employer but was a person involved in the
breach of employment standards. Section 142W sets out what is required for a person to be
deemed a “person involved in a breach”.
[18] In this case Mr Joost says each of Mr Miccio, Mr Win and Mr Whall were persons
involved in the breaches of employment standards because they were directors of APP and
because they were knowingly concerned in APP’s breaches of employment standards, applying
ss 142W(1)(c) and 142W (3)(c) of the Act.
[19] The effect of ss 142W(1)(c) and 142W(3)(c) of the Act was analysed by the Court of
Appeal in A Labour Inspector v Southern Taxis Limited and others.2 At paragraph [50] the
Court stated:
[50] Sections 142W and 142Y allocate, as between directors and other
officers on the one hand, and employees on the other hand, the risk that a
company will be unable to meet its minimum obligations under employment
legislation. The effect of these provisions is to impose the risk of non-
performance of those obligations by the company on a director who knows all
the primary facts relevant to the company’s breach, unless the director has
reasonably relied on information (for example, legal advice) provided by a
third party, or has taken all reasonable and proper steps to ensure the company
complied with the relevant provisions. ….
[20] The Court’s reference to reliance on information or taking reasonable steps comes from
s 142ZD of the Act, which sets out defences for persons involved in breaches of minimum
standards.
[21] So, based on ss 142W, 142Y and 142ZD of the Act and Southern Taxis the questions I
need to answer to resolve this employment relationship problem are:
2 A Labour Inspector v Southern Taxis Limited and Others [2021] NZCA 705.

(a) Has there been a breach of employment standards by APP resulting in a payment
being owed to Mr Joost?
(b) Were Mr Miccio, Mr Win and/or Mr Whall officers of APP?
(c) Did Mr Miccio, Mr Win and/or Mr Whall know the primary facts relevant to
APP’s breaches of employment standards?
(d) Did Mr Miccio, Mr Win and/or Mr Whall reasonably rely on information from
a third party, or did they take all reasonable steps to ensure APP complied with
the relevant employment standards?
Has there been a breach of employment standards by APP?
[22] Employment standards are set out in the Act. These are the minimum requirements to
be met by employers to employees and cover such things as the payment of minimum
entitlements under the Holidays Act 2003. Employment standards also include meeting the
provisions of the Wages Protection Act 1983; this means an employment standard is that
employers must pay employees their full wages or salary without making any unlawful
deductions.
[23] So, if Mr Joost was not paid his final two salary payments and his accrued holiday
entitlements then these failures by APP are breaches of employment standards.
[24] In this regard, Mr Joost says he was not paid the last two payments he was due from
APP:
(a) First, his normal fortnightly pay for the period 7 October 2024 – 20 October
2024. The net amount payable was $4,732.55. This should have been paid on 21
October 2024.
(b) Second, his final pay for the period 21 October 2024 – 23 October 2024 (which
amounted to one day of work and one day of annual leave) and his accrued but
untaken holiday entitlement. The net amount payable was $1,051.35 for the one
day of work and one day of annual leave, plus a gross amount of approximately
$13,000 for accrued but untaken holiday entitlement. This should have been paid
on 4 November 2025.

[25] Mr Miccio and Mr Winn produced two payslips issued by APP for Mr Joost that covered
these two payments:
(a) The payslip covering the first payment due to Mr Joost records that payment of
$4,732.55 was made to him on 29 October 2024 (the first payslip).
(b) The payslip covering the second payment due to Mr Joost records that payment
of $1,051.35 was made to him on 19 November 2025 (the second payslip). The
second payslip does not record any payment made for accrued holiday
entitlements, yet the accrued balance is recorded as zero – the first payslip had
accrued holiday entitlement at 3.74 weeks, which is $12,944.14
[26] Mr Miccio said in oral evidence that based on these two payslips he believed APP had
paid the salary owed to Mr Joost for the days worked or for which he had taken holidays, in the
two pay periods. I asked Mr Miccio about the accrued holiday entitlements and why it was
recorded as owing in the first payslip then reduced to zero in the second payslip without any
payment for that amount being paid to Mr Joost. Mr Miccio said that Mr Joost had taken several
days off work in the preceding months which had not been recorded as holidays; he believed
payroll had done a reconciliation of those days off with the accrued holiday entitlements and
the outcome must have been that Mr Joost had no accrued holiday entitlement left at the
termination of his employment.
[27] Mr Joost gave oral evidence in the investigation meeting, saying that despite what the
two payslips state about payment being made he did not receive any money from APP for these
two pays.
[28] I have reviewed Mr Joost’s evidence against that of Mr Miccio and Mr Winn, which is
limited as they do not have access to APP documents that are held by the Liquidator. I conclude
that Mr Joost’s evidence on non-payment of salary is credible and correct. I am largely
persuaded by two aspects of Mr Joost’s evidence – he made appropriate concessions throughout
his evidence and in particular about payments he did receive (albeit paid late by APP) and it
seems improbable that he would pursue a false claim against the three individual directors given
the cost implications weighed against the amount he was not paid.
[29] The position in respect of Mr Joost’s accrued holiday entitlements was not clear based
on the evidence. Mr Joost stated he had not received any payment for accrued but untaken

holiday entitlements at the end of his employment but could not say what that amount was. I
accept on Mr Miccio’s evidence that there was a basis by which APP decided that any accrued
amount of holiday entitlements recorded in the first pay slip was incorrect and a reconciliation
was necessary to account for leave Mr Joost had taken that had not been recorded as annual
leave at the time.
[30] So, for the purposes of establishing breaches of employment standards Mr Joost was not
paid the final two payments that he was due from APP. This covered salary and annual leave
for the relevant periods and an amount for accrued but untaken holiday entitlements – I cannot
however establish how much that should have been.
Were Mr Miccio, Mr Win and/or Mr Whall officers of APP?
[31] Mr Miccio, Mr Win and Mr Whall were directors of APP at the time of the breaches of
employment standards by APP; they are officers of APP for the purposes of s 142W of the Act.
Did Mr Miccio, Mr Win and/or Mr Whall know the primary facts relevant to the breaches
by APP?
[32] The position in respect of Mr Win and Mr Whall was clear based on the evidence I
heard. As non-executive directors of APP and based on the evidence about their involvement
in APP I find that they were not involved in day-to-day operations of APP. Consequently, in
the circumstances, they did know what employees were to be paid and whether payments were
being made. I accept that given their roles they were aware of the financial position of APP and
they took advice and direction from accountants as to APP’s ability to meet it outgoings
(discussed further below) but this was not sufficient for them to have knowledge of the primary
facts relevant to APP’s failure to pay Mr Joost his final two pays.
[33] Mr Miccio’s knowledge is less clear. At the relevant times he was the acting CEO and
his evidence was that in his role he authorised the wage and salary payments on request from
the APP payroll person. Mr Miccio was clear that he was not approving the amounts – he was
reliant on the APP payroll person and the payroll system to generate the correct amount, he
authorised the payments once he was notified of the payments and was satisfied they could be
made, i.e., he checked that payments were for salary or wages for employees and based on
advice on APP’s financial position (discussed further below) he then provided his authorisation
through the payroll system to allow payments to be made.

[34] Mr Miccio said that during this time, given APP’s difficult funding position, he and the
other directors were receiving advice from the accountants retained by APP regarding funding,
cashflow and outgoings, so he knew APP could continue operating as it could meet its
obligations. When that position changed APP was placed into voluntary administration; this
was on 20 November 2025, 16 days after the second pay was to be paid to Mr Joost.
[35] Having considered Mr Miccio’s evidence I conclude that he did not have knowledge of
the primary facts relevant to APP’s failure to pay Mr Joost his final two pays:
(a) He did not know the payments had not been paid at the time and at the
investigation meeting maintained the position that he believed, based on the first
payslip and the second payslip, that APP had paid Mr Joost. He knew there was
funding at the time to make these payments based on the advice from APP’s
accountants; it was for this reason that he authorised payment in his role as acting
CEO.
(b) He did not know what APP had decided about Mr Joost’s accrued but untaken
holiday entitlements; he assumed there had been a reconciliation and Mr Joost
was not owed anything but he was not privy to that reconciliation nor did he
approve it any way.
Did Mr Miccio, Mr Win and/or Mr Whall rely on advice or take reasonable steps to ensure
compliance?
[36] Given the evidence, I conclude that Mr Miccio, Mr Win and Mr Whall as members of
the APP Board of Directors took advice from accountants on APP’s funding, outgoings and
cashflow to be satisfied of its continued trading during the financial difficulties; it follows that
if I am wrong on the previous finding, each of Mr Miccio, Mr Win and Mr Whall would be able
to rely on the defence available under s 142ZD of the Act.

Summary and orders
[37] I determine that:
(a) APP breached employment standards by not paying Mr Joost his final two pays,
which should have included an amount for accrued holiday entitlements.
(b) Mr Miccio, Mr Win and Mr Whall were directors of APP at the time of the
breaches of employment standards and were officers of APP for the purposes of
s 142W of the Act.
(c) Mr Miccio, Mr Win and Mr Whall did not know all the primary facts relevant
to the breaches of employment standards by APP.
(d) And, in any event, Mr Miccio, Mr Win and Mr Whall relied on advice from
accountants regarding the revenue position of APP in respect of its continued
and ongoing operation at the time of the breaches and the defence available to
them pursuant to s 142ZD of the Act applies.
[38] Mr Miccio, Mr Win and Mr Whall are not liable for breaches of employment standards
by APP. This employment relationship problem is resolved in favour of Mr Miccio, Mr Win
and Mr Whall.
Costs
[39] Costs are reserved. The parties are encouraged to resolve any issue of costs between
themselves.
[40] If the parties are unable to resolve costs, and an Authority determination on costs is
needed, the respondents may lodge, and then should serve, a memorandum on costs within 28
days of the date of this determination. From the date of service of that memorandum Mr Joost
will then have 14 days to lodge any reply memorandum. On request by either party, an extension
of time for the parties to continue to negotiate costs between themselves may be granted.
